newsitem.title: UK: Oil price off after Turkey gives date for Iraq oil.
newsitem.headline: Oil price off after Turkey gives date for Iraq oil.

text.p: World oil prices reacted to news from Ankara that Iraqi crude oil would start flowing through the trans-Turkey pipeline by December 15 by shedding a few cents in thin volume on Thursday.
International benchmark Brent Blend crude oil from the North Sea for January delivery fell 15 cents just after the news to $22.60 a barrel, down 12 cents on the day.
The front-month contract had earlier traded in a tight range, rising to a high of $22.89 a barrel after OPEC ministers in Vienna agreed to freeze production to the end of June 1997.
"Volume is very, very thin," a floor trader said.

The bigger New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), was closed on Thursday and Friday for the Thanksgiving holiday, leaving London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) to bear the brunt of traders' reaction.
"People were just using this market in case any news came out from OPEC. It came off 15 cents and I think the market will come off from now on," the floor trader said.

Whether Brent will hold to current levels either side of $23 a barrel, which has been the case this week in anticipation of the OPEC meeting, will be known when NYMEX reopens on Monday, a trader said anticipating a further decline.
But a London-based broker thought the market had overreacted and pointed to views the tight winter market could absorb the additional Iraqi crude.
The Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) maintained its output ceiling at 25.03 million barrels per day (bpd), which includes provision for Iraqi oil sales of 800,000 bpd.

Most analysts saw a winter market absorbing the additional Iraqi oil if exports resumed in the first quarter of the year, when demand is traditionally high and particularly so with current low inventories.
Iraqi crude oil exports have been under a U.N. embargo since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in 1990 and the market had expected the first Iraqi exports to resume in September.

But these failed to materialise after Iraqi President Saddam Hussein sent troops into northern Iraq to intervene in Kurdish factional fighting, prompting a U.S. military response and postponement of the U.N. plan.
This made the market sceptical about any news of resumed Iraqi exports with some traders saying they would wait to see the oil on the water first.
Turkish State Minister Lutfi Esengun's said on Thursday that the pipeline from Iraq was ready and oil would flow to the Mediterranean export terminal at Ceyhan by December 15.

Iraq this week accepted U.N. conditions for the supervised oil sales and its chief OPEC delegate, Osama al-Hiti, told reporters in Vienna that Iraq would return to 1990 output levels of over 3.0 million bpd as soon as possible.

Such is the market's hunger for crude oil at present that it has been absorbing additional barrels from OPEC members producing above their quotas without a detrimental impact on prices, which remain some $3 a barrel above year-ago levels.

This was largely because consumer countries allowed inventories to run low on the assumption that Iraq would return to the market during the fourth quarter of this year and that non-OPEC supply would rise.
Neither happened and demand was stronger than forecast, allowing OPEC to reap the benefit of a price windfall without lifting a finger.
"OPEC are getting much better at taking the temperature of the market," said Bob Finch, the head of trading at Vitol SA, the world's biggest independent oil trading and refining company.

Earlier this week Iraq and the United Nations reached agreement on an "oil-for-food" deal that will allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion in oil over six months to buy food and medicines. The agreement is renewable.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) in Paris expects the call on OPEC oil to be 26.5 million bpd in the first quarter of 1997, compared to OPEC output of less than 26.0 million in recent months. This should allow room for most of the Iraqi oil at least during the winter months.
But analysts said the additional barrels could weigh on low demand seasons in the second and third quarters.
